full_judgment:
"15  Before a Court acts upon a confessional statement, it has to affirmatively satisfy that the statement is voluntary and true. In this regard, the judicial authorities always insist on the meticulous observance of all necessary formalities and precautions provided in section 164(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure with minute particularity so as to ensure that the confession is absolutely free from the slightest tinge or taint of extraneous influence. It is a settled principle of law as pointed out by a Division Bench of this Court in the case of Zaheda Bewa vs State reported in 1985 BLD 9 = 37 DLR 66 that the requirement of adherence to the provisions of section 164(3), CrPC is not a mere matter of form, but of substance. Section 164(3) is a mandatory provision of law as has been settled by the Privy Council in the case of Nazir Ahmed vs King Emperor, AIR 1936 PC 253. Before recording a confession, a Magistrate is bound to make a real and substantial enquiry as to the voluntariness of the confession. In so doing, he must put questions to the accused with a view to finding out the real object of the confession, whether it is made out of repentance or for any other such good reason or whether it is the result of torture or torturing by somebody or whether it has been caused by any inducement, threat or promise. The questions put by the Magistrate and the answers given by the accused furnish sufficient data for coming to the conclusion whether the statement was voluntary or not." 

 115. In the case of Nurul Haque vs State reported in 20 DLR 780, it has been observed: 

 "Now let us consider the value of a retracted confession as against the maker. On consideration of evidence on record, if it is found that a confession is voluntary  and true, conviction of the maker himself can solely be based upon the same, no matter whether it is retracted or not. In the case of the State vs Minbun reported in 16 DLR (SC) 598, their Lordships of the Supreme Court held as follows: 

 117. In the case of the State vs Punardhar Joydhar reported in 31 DLR 312, it has been held that the accused first made a confessional statement under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure that he committed the murder, although subsequently, he retracted his confessional statement before the Court and the confession being found voluntary and without any threat, coercion or inducement, conviction of the accused based on his confession, though subsequently retracted by him, is valid in law. 

 118. The principle that has been enunciated in the case of Hazrat Ali vs State reported in 1990 BLD 38 = 42 DLR 177 is that once a confession has been found to be true and voluntary, conviction can be based solely on the confession even if it is retracted. 

 119. The 'ratio decidendi' of the case of Bakul Chandra Sarkar vs State reported in 45 DLR 260 is that if a confession recorded under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is true and voluntary, the same alone is sufficient for convicting the confessing accused and retraction of confession is immaterial, once it is found to be true and voluntary. 

 120. In the decision in the case of Babul vs State reported in 42 DLR (AD) 186, it has been held, inter alia, in paragraph 10: 

 121. In the instant case, admittedly the Police Officer (PW 26) Md Abdul Quddus Khan who took the condemned-prisoners to the Magistrate or forwarded them for recording their confessions and the Magistrate himself (PW 15) Jagannath Das Khokan have been examined to prove that they made the confessions which were recorded and produced before the Court. By way of examination of the PW 15 Jagannath Das Khokan and the PW 26 Md Abdul Quddus Khan before the Court below, the prosecution has definitely brought on record the minimum legal evidence to prove the commission of the offence. In our view, the requirement of bringing the minimum legal evidence in this case has been fulfilled as mandated by our Appellate Division in the decision reported in 42 DLR (AD) 186 (Supra). 

 138. However, Md Abdul Baset Majumder has contended that since the initial intention of all the accused was to commit robbery at the place of occurrence, they cannot be fastened with the liability of committing culpable homicide amounting to murder punishable under section 302 of the Penal Code. In this connection, he has drawn our attention to the decisions in the case of Bandez Ali vs State reported in 40 DLR (AD) 200 and the case of State vs Tayeb Ali reported in 1987 BLWAD) 265 40 DLR (AD) 6. In contradistinction: to this contention. Mrs Maksuda Akhtar has referred to the decision in the case of the State  vs Montu reported in 44 DLR (AD) 287 and submitted that although there was no pre-plan of the accused to kill the victim in course of robbery; but the fact remains that their common intention to kill developed on the spot and in furtherance of that common intention, they caused the death of the victim. 

 140. It is true that common intention presupposes a preplan or a prior plan or a prior concert and a meeting of minds of the accused. But this common intention as contemplated by section 34 of the Penal Code may develop even on the spur of the moment and this view has been upheld by the decision reported in 44 DLR (AD) 287 referred to by Mrs Maksuda Akhtar. 

 144. From the confessional statements (Exhibits 15-18), it is manifest that the appellants, with a view to facilitating the commission of robbery, tied up the body of Sultana Khan Panni and her face with a scarf and pasted a Scotch tape on her mouth causing asphyxia resulting in her death. To put it differently, the appellants were hell-bent upon committing robbery at the place of occurrence even by causing her death. It is on record that she was a sexagenarian at the relevant time. As a sexagenarian, she was surely decrepit and suffered from old-age weakness. As an old lady, they were well aware of her physical state of health and bodily constitution. This being the position, it is easily deducible that the appellants knew that their criminal act was so imminently dangerous that it must, in all probability, cause such bodily injury as was likely to cause her death by shock and asphyxia and accordingly, they committed such act without any excuse for incurring the risk of causing such bodily injury as aforesaid thus attracting the ingredients of Clause '4thly' of section 300 of the Penal Code. So we opine that the criminal act of the appellants is culpable homicide amounting to murder. It may be remembered that as per opinion of the PW 17 Dr Md Nur Hossain, the death of the victim Sultana Khan Panni was due to the combined effect of shock and asphyxia as a result of the injuries found by him during autopsy which wee ante-mortem and homicidal in nature. The decisions reported in 40 DLR (AD) 200 and 1987 BLD (AD) 265 have no manner of application to the instant case, inasmuch 'as the facts and circumstances of tile cases are quite distinguishable. As such, those' decisions do not help Mr Majumder in any way.
